books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom”

stimulus.text:
“The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line,—the relation of the darker to the lighter races of men in Asia and Africa, in America and the islands of the sea. It was a phase of this problem that caused the Civil War; and however much they who marched South and North in 1861 may have fixed on the technical points, of union and local autonomy as a shibboleth, all nevertheless knew, as we know, that the question of Negro slavery was the real cause of the conflict.”

—W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom”
stimulus.source_note: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom.” Public domain (Project Gutenberg eBook #408). Wording verified against the Gutenberg text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Du Bois’s chapter “Of the Dawn of Freedom” studies the years 1861 to 1872. Which of the following best explains why a historian of Reconstruction would open with the color-line rather than with a battle or a law?

options.text: Du Bois believed that battles and laws did not matter.
options.misconception: The chapter is full of laws and institutions, the Bureau and the amendments; Du Bois weighs them carefully.

options.text: The color-line explains why emancipation alone could not finish the work.
Du Bois had no sources for the battles and laws.
options.misconception: Background: Du Bois was a trained historian with full access to the record; the choice is interpretive, not a gap.

options.text: The color-line was a phrase invented by the Supreme Court.
options.misconception: Background: the phrase is Du Bois’s own, from this book.

rationales.A: The chapter is full of laws and institutions, the Bureau and the amendments; Du Bois weighs them carefully.
rationales.B: Laws freed the slaves and made them citizens, but the line between Black and white kept shaping who could vote, learn, and earn. Du Bois opens with the line because it is the reason the laws were not enough.
rationales.C: Background: Du Bois was a trained historian with full access to the record; the choice is interpretive, not a gap.
rationales.D: Background: the phrase is Du Bois’s own, from this book.
rationales.general:
1. A battle or a law would tell the story of one event; Du Bois wants the story of the whole era.
2. The color-line is his answer to why emancipation did not end the struggle.
3. Laws changed status, but the line still decided who could vote, learn, and earn.
4. Opening with the line tells the reader what to watch for in every law that follows.
Remember: historians open with the cause that explains the rest, not with the first event on the timeline.
